findings.section: whole file; also 4-say.md, 1-fast.md#look-first-3-min and the Try it callouts in 2-deep.md
findings.quote:
# Amazon DynamoDB: do it

Nothing here yet.
findings.evidence: Rule broken: TOOLS-items.md sync: 'Only items with `status: ready` are printed ... A file with no item still gets its H1 and the line `Nothing here yet.`' and TOOLS-rules.md set-status: 'A reviewer sets cards, speak items and tasks to `ready` in the stage of that kind, after the item lint is clean.' data/28-dynamodb/tasks.json has 3 items, speak.json 4 and cards.json 32, all with status candidate and none ready (chapters 26 and 27 have their speak items and tasks set to ready). Effect for the reader: 3-do.md and 4-say.md are empty, the Look first task region in 1-fast.md (<!-- task:start id=dynamodb-t01 --><!-- task:end -->) is empty, and the two 'See [3-do.md](3-do.md)' links in 2-deep.md lead to an empty page. She gets no spoken answers and no hands-on tasks, which she asked for. Fix: run tasks/speak/cards lint and set-status ready, then sync.
findings.resolution: fix-28: same fix as claims-01: all tasks, speak items and cards set to ready after clean item lints; sync 28 printed 3-do.md, 4-say.md and the task region.

findings.quote: ### DAX answers repeated eventually consistent reads from memory in microseconds (4 min) ... **Stop and answer.** A leaderboard rereads the same 100 items all day with eventually consistent reads. Does DAX fit?
findings.evidence: READER.md: 'Headings, tables and captions must give a correct gist on their own; questions must test what the gist misses.' The assertion heading alone answers these Stop-and-answer items: 'A table stores items and each item needs only its primary key' (do all items need the same attributes?), 'A hash of the partition key picks the partition so hot keys throttle' (can purchases on one counter item be throttled?), 'DAX answers repeated eventually consistent reads ...' (does DAX fit repeated eventually consistent reads?), 'In a global table every replica accepts reads and writes' (what changes in the database when us-east-1 is impaired?). In 1-fast.md, Check 2 (can a GSI read be strongly consistent?) is answered by the compare table row 'Strongly consistent reads? | No: queries support eventual consistency only'. Rewrite these items so they need a step the heading does not give (for example the 1,000 write units ceiling and the sharding fix, a write-heavy or strong-read twist for DAX, the routing change for the global table).
findings.resolution: fix-28: four deep Stop-and-answer items now need a step the heading does not give: item size (photos past 400 KB go to S3), the hot key fix (what do you change: shard the key), DAX with reads that must show the latest score (strong reads pass through), and the global table (what must the team do: route users; no database failover). Fast Check 2 kept: the Check section re-tests the compare tables by design and its reveal also carries Predict 2.

findings.quote: **Figure.** A write lands in the partition that the key's hash picks, and DynamoDB copies it to three Availability Zones before it confirms the write.
findings.evidence: The same picture then says 'A later read is eventually consistent unless it asks for a strong read', and step 5 links dynamodb-eventually-consistent-default. A reader who trusts the caption asks: if all three copies exist before the write is confirmed, why can a later read miss it? The chapter never gives the cause, so the gist is self-contradictory. Facts in play: dynamodb-faq-sync-replication-three-azs, dynamodb-successful-write-http-200-durable, dynamodb-eventually-consistent-may-lag ('might not reflect the results of a recently completed write operation'). Either soften the caption to the FAQ wording (replicates across three Availability Zones; HTTP 200 means durable) or add one grounded cause-and-effect sentence on why an eventually consistent read can lag. The spoken answer s04 repeats the claim ('copied to three Availability Zones before DynamoDB confirms it').
findings.resolution: fix-28: caption softened as claims-06; the spec claim changed and the SVG was rebuilt. Hero step 5 keeps the eventually consistent default with its fact, so the caption no longer implies that every copy exists before success.

findings.quote: **The problem it solves.** A relational database holds a connection and row locks per client, so one server sets the ceiling. [DynamoDB uses an HTTP API](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-ddb-http-api-no-connections) and spreads items over partitions.
findings.evidence: Reader lens rule: a mechanism must be told as cause and effect. The paragraph names two features and leaves out the effect (why an HTTP API without held connections plus partitions removes the single-server ceiling). 'row locks per client' is also not how locks work (a lock is held on the rows a transaction changes, not per client), so the cause it gives is misleading. Rewrite as: cause (each client holds a connection; concurrent updates of one row wait on its lock) -> effect (one server's connection limit and lock queue cap the work) -> DynamoDB's answer (each request is a stateless HTTP call, fact lambda-ddb-http-api-no-connections; items spread over partitions by key hash, fact dynamodb-partition-key-hash-decides-partition).
findings.resolution: fix-28: rewritten as cause and effect with the Lambda fact (see claims-10); 'row locks per client' removed.

findings.quote: For an item read as [12 KB](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-getitem-round-10kb-example), AWS prices:
findings.evidence: Both linked facts are about a 10 KB item: dynamodb-getitem-round-10kb-example quote 'If you read an item of 10 KB, DynamoDB rounds the item size to 12 KB.' and dynamodb-pricing-provisioned-10kb-example quote 'an eventually consistent read of a 10 KB item would require 1.5 RCUs (0.5 x 3)'. 'An item read as 12 KB' hides the rounding step, which is the point of the example and of Question 5. Say: 'A 10 KB item rounds up to 12 KB, three blocks of 4 KB:' then the table.
findings.resolution: fix-28: 'An item that rounds up to [12 KB], three blocks of [4 KB], costs:' (see claims-20).

findings.quote: 3. **Scale in minutes.** Auto scaling acts after a breach of [two consecutive minutes](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-autoscaling-two-consecutive-minutes)
findings.evidence: 'A breach' of what? The target utilization that auto scaling tracks is never introduced, yet Question 12 uses 'auto scaling at a 70% target utilization'. Fact dynamodb-autoscaling-two-consecutive-minutes quote: 'Auto scaling triggers when your consumed capacity breaches the configured target utilization for two consecutive minutes.' Name the target utilization (the share of provisioned capacity that auto scaling aims to keep in use) and say it in that order.
findings.resolution: fix-28: step 3 now names it first: 'Auto scaling aims at a [target utilization], the share of capacity in use. It acts when use stays above it for [two consecutive minutes]...' (verified fact dynamodb-autoscaling-target-utilization).

findings.quote: Throttled requests. The AWS SDKs [automatically retry requests that receive this exception](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-sdk-retries-throttled-requests).
findings.evidence: 'this exception' refers to nothing in the chapter: no exception is named before it. The fact dynamodb-sdk-retries-throttled-requests has the claim 'requests that receive a provisioned throughput exceeded exception'. Name ProvisionedThroughputExceededException once (it is also the word she will see in a customer's logs), or rephrase the display around 'throttled requests'.
findings.resolution: fix-28: the dangling SDK retry sentence ('this exception') was removed; the new answer (claims-05) names throttled requests and burst capacity and needs no exception name.

findings.quote: Before a launch far above any earlier peak, raise the **warm throughput** ([pre-warming](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-warm-throughput-prewarm-for-peak-events)).
findings.evidence: The term is bolded as a new term but never defined in the prose; only Question 12's explanation defines it (fact dynamodb-warm-throughput-definition, 'can instantaneously support'). Question 12 and speak s01 both depend on it. Add the one-line definition from dynamodb-warm-throughput-definition here.
findings.resolution: fix-28: the trap now defines it: 'The **warm throughput** is what a table [can instantaneously support]' (dynamodb-warm-throughput-definition), then pre-warming, with the change date [November 13, 2024].

findings.quote: The other mode is **multi-Region strong consistency** (MRSC).
findings.evidence: MRSC is named and placed in a table (Regions, RPO) but what it does is never said: what a read returns, what happens to conflicting writes, why it needs exactly three Regions or a witness. She cannot explain it to a customer from this page. Facts available: dynamodb-gt-mrsc-exactly-three-regions (quote: 'You can configure a MRSC global table with three replicas, or with two replicas and one witness.'), dynamodb-dr-global-tables-mrsc-rpo-zero, dynamodb-global-tables-consistency-mode-fixed. One plain sentence of cause and effect is enough.
findings.resolution: fix-28: one sentence added: 'In multi-Region strong consistency (MRSC), writes are [synchronously replicated to at least one other Region]: strong reads [always return the latest version of an item]' (dynamodb-gt-mrsc-synchronous-latest-reads); the table names the witness option.

findings.quote: A global table needs no restore: its **recovery time objective** is an [RTO of zero](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-dr-global-tables-mrec-rto-zero).
findings.evidence: RPO gets a plain meaning ('The **recovery point objective** (RPO) is the data you can lose.'), RTO gets only its name. The edit note in the ledger says 'RTO defined at first use', but only the expansion is there. STYLE rule: define a term at first use. Add the parallel line: the RTO is how long the application can be down.
findings.resolution: fix-28: 'its recovery time objective (RTO), the time the application is down, is an [RTO of zero]'.

findings.quote:
**Options.**

- A larger PostgreSQL instance for the job rows.
- Amazon DynamoDB with on-demand capacity.
- Amazon ElastiCache for job state.
findings.evidence: SPEC.json decision record words max 280; lint W201 in the ledger: 'Decision record has 325 words; the section allows 0 to 280'. At the same time the record never says why the two rejected options lose (the larger instance keeps the same connection and lock ceiling; ElastiCache is an ephemeral cache, fact dynamodb-decision-guide-elasticache-caching-layer), so the reader gets the answer without the reasoning that the exam tests. The numbered lists under the two figures repeat the captions nearly word for word; cut them and spend the words on one reason per rejected option.
findings.resolution: fix-28: each rejected option now has its reason ('updates still wait on row locks'; ElastiCache is an [ephemeral cache for frequently accessed data], not a job record). The two numbered lists stay: L703 requires the four spec steps under each figure (removing them failed lint). The section stays above 280 words (W201, warning).

findings.quote: > **The exam probably expects:** on-demand for spiky, provisioned for steady traffic. Prefer an option right under both.
findings.evidence: RULINGS hard rule 8 (plain English, no idioms). 'Prefer an option right under both' is not clear to a second-language reader: it means 'choose an answer that is correct under both the old and the new pricing'. Say that.
findings.resolution: fix-28: now 'Choose an answer that is right under old and new prices.'

findings.quote: Why one partition? Idle capacity elsewhere does not help a hot key.
findings.evidence: The 'Why' line restates the effect instead of giving a cause, and the chapter never mentions adaptive capacity, while speak item s03 has the follow-up 'Doesn't DynamoDB fix a hot key by itself?' answered 'Partly. Adaptive capacity rebalances partitions so that frequently accessed items don't reside on the same partition.' (fact dynamodb-adaptive-capacity-isolates-hot-items). She will be asked that follow-up and cannot answer it from the chapter. Give the cause (one item or one key value lives in one partition, and one partition has a fixed ceiling, fact dynamodb-partition-max-throughput) and one sentence on what adaptive capacity does and does not do.
findings.resolution: fix-28: the Why line now gives the cause and adaptive capacity: 'Each item lives in one partition. Adaptive capacity [rebalances your partitions] to split hot items, but one hot item still meets its ceiling.' The Stop and answer adds the 1,000 write units ceiling and the sharding fix.

findings.quote: > **Try it:** Compare a Query and a Scan by consumed capacity. See [3-do.md](3-do.md). <!-- task: dynamodb-t02 -->
findings.evidence: tasks.json dynamodb-t02 step 6 expect: 'With three tiny items, Units can equal the value of the Scan.' The task promises a comparison by consumed capacity, but with three items of a few bytes every call rounds to the same units, so the hands-on result shows no capacity difference between Query and Scan; only ScannedCount differs. A reader who acts before she reads may conclude that a Query costs the same as a Scan. Either write enough item data that the Scan crosses the next 4 KB read block (still $0 in practice) or retitle the Try line to compare ScannedCount.
findings.resolution: fix-28: Try line retitled to what the task shows: 'Watch a filter leave a Scan's units unchanged; compare ScannedCount with a Query.' The task itself (verified, ready) is unchanged.

findings.quote: None: reserved capacity is not for Standard-IA tables [or on-demand capacity mode]
findings.evidence: Standard-IA appears in the fast file only here, unexplained; the table class is introduced only later in 2-deep (TTL subsection). STYLE: define a term at first use, or drop the clause from the fast file.
findings.resolution: fix-28: kept. The cell must hold a display of dynamodb-reserved-capacity-not-for-ia-on-demand, and both displays name Standard-IA; the new signals row in the same file ('storage is most of the bill' -> the Standard-IA table class) explains the class, and the fast file is at 1,800 words.

findings.quote: **Check 3.** Users in us-east-1 and eu-west-1 change the same item at the same moment. ... The later one: by default, [last writer wins]
findings.evidence: 'At the same moment' and 'the later one' contradict each other for a literal reader. Say 'within the same second' or 'almost at the same time'. Fact dynamodb-gt-mrec-default-last-writer-wins.
findings.resolution: fix-28: Check 3 now says 'almost at the same time'.

findings.quote: In AWS CloudShell, read the throughput quotas of your account and of one table, and list your tables.
findings.evidence: 'Throughput' and capacity units are first explained in the Words table and in 2-deep, after this task. The task text also says 'list your tables', but tasks.json dynamodb-t01 has no list-tables step. The belief it kills ('A DynamoDB table has no throughput limit') is about table quotas, which the exam rarely tests; the per-partition ceiling (dynamodb-partition-max-throughput) is the belief that matters and cannot be seen with describe-limits.
findings.resolution: fix-28: Look first no longer promises 'list your tables'; it now matches the task (account and new-table quotas, in two Regions). The belief the task kills is a task-stage choice that passed its gate; the per-partition ceiling is not visible through describe-limits, so the task is not changed.

findings.quote: the eu-west-1 replica table adds [one rWRU per replica table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gt-rwru-per-replica) for every write
findings.evidence: rWRU (replicated write request unit) is not defined anywhere in the chapter. STYLE: no unexplained abbreviation. Spell it out once or say 'a replicated write charge in each extra Region'.
findings.resolution: fix-28: dynamodb-q012 option c why only: 'adds a replicated write request unit (rWRU) charge, [one rWRU per replica table] for every write'.

findings.quote: **Stop and answer.** A team disables a table's customer managed key and forgets it for a week. What happens?
findings.evidence: Fact dynamodb-customer-managed-key-inaccessible-archived: 'for longer than seven days, the table is archived'. 'For a week' sits exactly on the boundary, so the answer's second sentence does not follow from the stem. Say 'for two weeks'. Also in this subsection, 'Why IAM? The role of your code then carries its table permissions.' does not answer the why.
findings.resolution: fix-28: stem now 'for two weeks'; Why line now 'Your code's role carries its permissions, so no password is stored.'

findings.quote: | [1 MB per call](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-query-result-1mb) | One Query or Scan page | Larger results need paging |
findings.evidence: Paging (pagination with a last evaluated key) is not explained anywhere in the chapter, so the 'why it decides' cell is a new idea in a numbers table. One clause in the Query subsection is enough.
findings.resolution: fix-28: A-list cell now 'Ask for more with `LastEvaluatedKey`' (the fact's own wording).

findings.quote: For DynamoDB caching, DAX or ElastiCache: which one supports lists, sets and hashes? || ElastiCache.
findings.evidence: Three cards test what the chapter never teaches: c024 (data structures of ElastiCache), c030 ('dynamodb:LeadingKeys, with the ForAllValues modifier': ForAllValues does not appear in the chapter), c032 ('BatchWriteItem does not support UpdateItem requests'). A card should recall something she has read; either add one clause to the prose or swap the card.
findings.resolution: fix-28: c030 taught in IAM step 2 (ForAllValues); c032 taught in the BatchWriteItem trap ('it [does not support] `UpdateItem` requests', dynamodb-batchwriteitem-no-updateitem); c024 taught by the new DAX/ElastiCache compare row 'Queries beyond key-value access?' ([ElastiCache (Redis OSS) supports advanced data structures]).
